adam.name: Adam
adam.feast_note: Traditional Christmas Eve commemoration with Eve; this is not a universal Roman-calendar feast.
adam.origin: The garden of Eden in Genesis
adam.dates: Biblical figure; no historical date assigned
biography: Adam belongs to the creation and fall narratives of Genesis. The account presents him with Eve in the garden of Eden, describes their disobedience to God, and tells of their expulsion from the garden. Its religious concerns include humanity’s relationship with God, moral responsibility, work, suffering, and mortality.

Christian interpretation reads this story in relation to redemption: the USCCB’s notes explain the tradition of seeing Genesis 3:15 as a promise of a redeemer. Adam and Eve are traditionally remembered on Christmas Eve in some Christian devotional calendars. This is a biblical and theological account, not a modern biography with independently established birth and death dates.

sources.title: USCCB: Genesis 3 and explanatory notes

richard-of-chichester.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
richard-of-chichester.name: Richard of Chichester
biography: Richard, also known as Richard de Wyche, studied at Oxford, Paris, and Bologna and served as a church administrator before becoming bishop of Chichester. His election met opposition from Henry III, who withheld the revenues of the diocese even after Pope Innocent IV consecrated him in 1245.

For a time Richard depended on the hospitality of his clergy while carrying out his ministry. His later work included preaching in support of a crusade. He died at Dover on April 3, 1253, and was buried at Chichester. Canonized in 1262, he is remembered through early biographies and his surviving will. April 3, rather than February 7, is the feast recorded by the cited source.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Richard de Wyche

catherine-de-ricci.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
catherine-de-ricci.name: Catherine de Ricci
biography: Catherine was born Alessandra de Ricci in Florence and entered the Dominican community at San Vincenzo in Prato as a teenager. She became a prioress and remained involved in the guidance of her community and in correspondence with people seeking spiritual advice.

Her reputation was closely associated with reported mystical experiences of Christ’s Passion. These belong to the devotional accounts of her religious life, alongside the documented history of her community leadership. She was canonized in 1746. The cited Dominican calendar observes her on February 4; the Roman Martyrology records her on February 2, the anniversary of her death.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Catherine de’ Ricci
Nominis: Sainte Catherine de Ricci

catherine-labour.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
catherine-labour.name: Catherine Labouré
biography: Catherine Labouré joined the Daughters of Charity in 1830. While a novice in Paris, she reported apparitions of Mary associated with the design of the Miraculous Medal. The medal became widely known while Catherine herself continued a largely hidden life of service.

Assigned to the hospice at Reuilly in 1831, she cared for elderly people and fulfilled ordinary community duties for decades. Her life therefore includes both the reported visions and a long record of practical charity. She died on December 31, 1876. Her November 28 commemoration is distinct from the anniversary of her death.

sources.title: Chapel of Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal: Catherine Labouré
Society of St. Vincent de Paul reflection: Feast of Saint Catherine Labouré

catherine-of-alexandria.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
catherine-of-alexandria.name: Catherine of Alexandria
biography: Catherine of Alexandria is venerated as a virgin and martyr whose legend became especially influential in medieval Christianity. It portrays a learned young woman who defended the Christian faith before an emperor and his scholars, endured imprisonment, and was condemned to death.

The surviving narratives contain substantial legendary development, including the breaking of a torture wheel and the miraculous transfer of her body to Sinai. They do not provide a secure contemporary biography. Her wheel, learning, and martyr’s palm became familiar features of Christian art. Her November 25 feast preserves a longstanding devotion while the details of her historical life remain uncertain.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Catherine of Alexandria

catherine-of-genoa.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
catherine-of-genoa.name: Catherine of Genoa
biography: Catherine Fieschi entered an arranged marriage at sixteen and experienced a difficult period before a profound religious conversion in 1473. Her later life joined contemplative prayer with work at Genoa’s Pammatone Hospital, where she cared for the sick and helped direct the institution.

Her husband eventually joined her in that service. The spiritual teaching associated with Catherine was preserved and edited by people around her rather than simply published as an autobiography. Her account of purgatory emphasizes purification through divine love, not a geographical tour of the afterlife. She continued her service to the sick until her death in 1510.

sources.title: Benedict XVI: Saint Catherine of Genoa
Nominis: Sainte Catherine de Gênes

catherine-of-siena.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
catherine-of-siena.name: Catherine of Siena
biography: Catherine joined the Dominican lay religious tradition while continuing to live at home in Siena. Her life combined prayer, care for people who were poor or sick, and spiritual guidance for a growing circle of followers.

Her letters and journeys brought her into public church affairs. She urged Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome and later supported Urban VI during the Western Schism. The Dialogue preserves her influential spiritual teaching. Recognized as a Doctor of the Church and a co-patron of Europe, she is remembered for both contemplative devotion and active engagement with the divisions of her time.

sources.title: Benedict XVI: Saint Catherine of Siena
Vatican News: Sainte Catherine de Sienne

cecilia.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
cecilia.name: Cecilia
cecilia.dates: Early Christian period; precise dates uncertain
biography: Cecilia is one of Rome’s best-known early martyrs and is honored as a patron of church music. Evidence for her veneration includes early liturgical records, her association with the Catacomb of Callistus, and the ancient church dedicated to her in Trastevere.

The detailed story of her marriage, the conversion of her husband, and her martyrdom comes through later accounts whose chronology is difficult to establish. These traditions have deeply influenced art and music, but do not justify a precise modern reconstruction of every event. Her feast on November 22 is connected with the Roman church that bears her name.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Cecilia

charbel-makhlouf.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
charbel-makhlouf.name: Charbel Makhlouf
biography: Charbel was a Maronite monk who joined the Lebanese Maronite Order in 1851, made his vows in 1853, and was ordained a priest in 1859. After years in community at Annaya, he became a hermit, devoting the remainder of his life to prayer, work, and ascetic discipline.

He died on Christmas Eve in 1898. Reports of extraordinary events and healings associated with his tomb contributed to the growth of pilgrimage there. Paul VI beatified him in 1965 and canonized him in 1977. His Roman-calendar memorial is July 24. Charbel and Sharbel are spellings of the same name, not two different saints.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Charbel Makhlouf and the Annaya monastery
Vatican News: July 24 calendar

charles-borromeo.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
charles-borromeo.name: Charles Borromeo
biography: Charles Borromeo studied civil and canon law before becoming a priest and bishop in 1563. He was closely involved in the Catholic reform associated with the Council of Trent and contributed to the work that produced its catechism.

After taking up residence in Milan, he made repeated pastoral visits, organized diocesan life, and established seminaries to improve the formation of priests. His work also included schools, hospitals, and assistance to people in need. His legacy is especially connected with putting church reform into practical effect through the responsibilities of a resident bishop.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Charles Borromeo

andrew-corsini.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
andrew-corsini.name: Andrew Corsini
biography: Andrew Corsini entered the Carmelites and served as their provincial before becoming bishop of Fiesole in 1349. His reputation for charity had grown during the plague at Florence, and he carried that concern for others into his episcopal ministry.

He also undertook work as a mediator, including a papal mission to settle disputes in Bologna. The account published by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints emphasizes his preaching, prayer, and practical example. His commemoration appears on January 9 in the cited Vatican calendar; February 4 is found in the older Roman calendar.

Vatican City State: January 9, Saint Andrew Corsini
Older Roman liturgy: Saint Andrew Corsini

anthony-mary-claret.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anthony-mary-claret.name: Anthony Mary Claret
biography: Anthony Mary Claret grew up in a textile-working family in Catalonia and trained in that trade before entering the seminary. Ordained in 1835, he moved from parish service into itinerant preaching, combining missionary travel with the distribution of religious publications.

In 1849 he founded the Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, now known as the Claretians. He was subsequently appointed archbishop of Santiago de Cuba and consecrated in 1850. His later life ended in exile in France, where he died on October 24, 1870. Pope Pius XII canonized him in 1950.

anthony-mary-zaccaria.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anthony-mary-zaccaria.name: Anthony Mary Zaccaria
biography: Anthony Mary Zaccaria was born in Cremona and trained in medicine before becoming a priest. His religious work centered on renewal of Christian life through preaching, prayer, and communities inspired by the apostle Paul.

He helped establish the Barnabites in 1533 and the Angelic Sisters in 1535, connecting the work of priests, religious women, and laypeople. His short life left institutions that continued beyond his death in 1539. Leo XIII canonized him in 1897, and his feast is July 5. Reports of extraordinary experiences belong to his devotional biography and should not replace the documented history of his foundations.

agnes-le-thi-thanh.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
agnes-le-thi-thanh.name: Agnes Lê Thị Thành
biography: Agnes Lê Thị Thành, also known as Dê, was a Vietnamese laywoman and mother who sheltered a priest during persecution. Her support for the Christian community led to her arrest, mistreatment, and death in prison.

She is included among the 117 Vietnamese martyrs canonized by John Paul II in 1988. The Holy See’s official list records her death on July 12, 1841; some devotional listings give a different year. This profile follows the canonization list for that date. Her witness belongs to the history of lay Catholics who risked their lives to sustain the Church under persecution.

sources.title: Holy See: Official list of the 117 martyrs of Vietnam
Nominis: Sainte Agnès Lê Thi Than

barnabas.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
barnabas.name: Barnabas
biography: Barnabas was a Jewish Levite from Cyprus who joined the early Christian community in Jerusalem. Acts describes him selling a field to support the community. He later worked with Paul at Antioch and accompanied him on a missionary journey through Cyprus and parts of Asia Minor.

Their partnership included disagreement: Barnabas wanted to take John Mark on a further journey, while Paul objected. Barnabas returned to Cyprus with Mark. The New Testament provides substantial evidence for his missionary work but does not give a complete account of his later life. His June 11 feast honors a missionary collaborator whose story also shows the human challenges of shared ministry.

sources.title: Benedict XVI: Barnabas, Silas, and Apollos
Vatican News: June 11 calendar

bruno.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bruno.name: Bruno of Cologne
biography: Bruno was a teacher at the cathedral school of Reims before seeking a more secluded religious life. In 1084 he and six companions received help from Hugh of Grenoble to establish a community in the mountains of the Chartreuse.

The form of life that developed there combined solitude with shared worship and became the foundation of the Carthusian tradition. Bruno later lived in Italy and died on October 6, 1101. The Carthusians preserve his memory through their own historical records and surviving writings. Leo X authorized his liturgical veneration in 1514, and it was later extended to the wider Church.

sources.title: Carthusian nuns: Saint Bruno, with historical references

basil-the-great.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
basil-the-great.name: Basil the Great
biography: Basil was a bishop of Caesarea and a major fourth-century theologian. Raised in a Christian family that included several other saints, he studied in Caesarea, Constantinople, and Athens before turning toward ascetic life. He visited monastic communities and developed a form of communal religious life in Pontus.

He became bishop in 370 and defended the Church’s teaching on the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit. His writings, pastoral correspondence, and guidance for monastic communities gave him a lasting influence in Eastern Christianity. He is distinguished from his father, Basil the Elder. In the Roman calendar he shares a January 2 memorial with Gregory of Nazianzus.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Basil the Great
Vatican News: January 2 calendar

bernard-of-clairvaux.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bernard-of-clairvaux.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
biography: Bernard entered the Cistercian monastery at Cîteaux and went on to lead the foundation at Clairvaux. His preaching and writings helped make the Cistercian reform influential across Europe. His spiritual teaching emphasized love of Christ, contemplation, and the relationship between prayer and monastic life.

His influence also extended into disputed church elections and political affairs. He supported Innocent II during a papal schism and preached the Second Crusade, an important and difficult part of his historical legacy. A balanced account therefore includes both the contemplative writer and the public churchman involved in the conflicts of his century.

sources.title: Vatican News: Saint Bernard
Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Bernard of Clairvaux

bernardine-of-siena.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bernardine-of-siena.name: Bernardine of Siena
biography: Bernardine helped care for the sick during the plague at Siena in 1400 before entering the Franciscans. He became associated with the Observant movement, which sought to renew the order’s commitment to poverty and its original religious discipline.

As a preacher, he addressed large crowds in language drawn from ordinary life, using memorable examples to communicate religious teaching. His ministry took him through many Italian cities and linked preaching with reform of Franciscan communities. Exhausted during a final preaching journey, he died at L’Aquila in 1444. His memorial falls on May 20.

sources.title: Vatican News: Saint Bernardin de Sienne

blaise.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
blaise.name: Blaise of Sebaste
biography: Blaise is remembered as a bishop and martyr of Sebaste. His traditional account describes a physician who became a bishop and was killed after refusing to renounce Christianity. Much of his familiar story comes through later devotional tradition rather than a detailed contemporary biography.

The best-known episode tells of a child delivered from a fish bone lodged in his throat. This story explains Blaise’s particular association with prayers for those suffering from throat ailments and the blessing of throats on his feast. The Catholic calendar commemorates him on February 3.

sources.title: Vatican News: February 3 calendar

blandina.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
blandina.name: Blandina of Lyon
biography: Blandina was an enslaved Christian among the martyrs of Lyon in 177. A letter from the local churches, preserved by Eusebius, records the persecution and describes how prisoners supported one another through interrogation and suffering.

The account emphasizes Blandina’s steadfastness despite her physical vulnerability. She was repeatedly brought into the arena before being killed. Her memory is therefore grounded in an early account of a particular persecuted community, rather than only in later legend. Her feast is June 2, together with the remembrance of the martyrs of Lyon.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Blandina

bonaventure.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bonaventure.name: Bonaventure
biography: Born Giovanni Fidanza, Bonaventure studied at Paris and entered the Franciscan Order. He became a theologian and teacher before being elected minister general in 1257. In that office he worked to guide an expanding order through disagreements about how to live Francis of Assisi’s ideal.

He wrote the Legenda Major, an influential life of Francis, as well as theological and spiritual works. Pope Gregory X made him a cardinal and bishop of Albano, and he helped prepare the Council of Lyon, where he died in 1274. The Church later recognized him as a Doctor of the Church, traditionally called the Seraphic Doctor.

sources.title: Vatican News: Saint Bonaventure

boniface.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
boniface.name: Boniface
biography: Boniface, originally named Winfrid, was an English monk and teacher who undertook missionary work on the European continent. His first journey to Frisia in 716 met political obstacles, but he returned to his missionary vocation after seeking authorization in Rome.

Known as the Apostle of Germany, he combined preaching with the organization of dioceses and the development of church life. His learning is reflected in his correspondence as well as his teaching. He died as a martyr in the mid-eighth century, and his remains came to rest at Fulda. His commemoration is June 5.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Boniface
Vatican News: June 5 calendar

boris-of-bulgaria.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
boris-of-bulgaria.name: Boris of Bulgaria
biography: Boris, who received the name Michael at baptism, was the Bulgarian ruler associated with the establishment of Christianity in his country. His reign involved difficult relations with neighboring powers and with both Rome and Constantinople as Bulgaria’s church organization developed.

He eventually withdrew to a monastery, but returned to political action when his successor Vladimir rejected Christianity. Boris replaced him with Simeon before resuming monastic life. Orthodox tradition honors him as Equal of the Apostles and commemorates him on May 2. His religious legacy should be understood alongside the exercise of royal power, rather than as a purely private conversion story.

sources.title: Orthodox Church in America: Saint Boris

brendan-the-navigator.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
brendan-the-navigator.name: Brendan the Navigator
biography: Brendan of Clonfert, also known as Brendan the Voyager, belonged to the early Irish monastic tradition. Accounts associate him with religious foundations in Ireland, especially Clonfert, and with travel undertaken for religious purposes.

His wider fame comes from the Navigatio, the medieval narrative of a voyage in search of a promised land. Its extraordinary islands and encounters belong to religious literature and legend. The story is important for medieval culture, but it does not prove that Brendan reached North America or establish a reliable route for such a voyage. His feast is May 16.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Brendan

bridget-of-sweden.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bridget-of-sweden.name: Bridget of Sweden
biography: Bridget, also called Birgitta, was married to Ulf Gudmarsson and raised eight children. After a pilgrimage with her husband and his subsequent death, she devoted herself more fully to religious life. Her reported revelations, recorded and translated with the help of clerical advisers, became influential in medieval Christianity.

She founded the Order of the Savior, known as the Bridgettines, and traveled to Rome to seek approval for its rule. Her work included charitable service and calls for church reform, including an appeal for the papacy to return from Avignon to Rome. She died in 1373 and was canonized in 1391.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Bridget of Sweden

brigid-of-ireland.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
brigid-of-ireland.name: Brigid of Kildare
biography: Brigid is remembered as the abbess associated with Kildare, whose name means church of the oak. The religious community connected with her became an important center of worship and learning, and she came to hold a prominent place in Irish Christian devotion.

Her surviving Lives preserve accounts of generosity, religious leadership, and miracles, but they differ in their details and were written after her lifetime. Precise dates and individual episodes should therefore be treated with care. The history of devotion to her and of Kildare’s community is more secure than every story attached to her name. Her feast is February 1.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Brigid of Ireland

cajetan.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
cajetan.name: Cajetan
biography: Cajetan, also known as Gaetano, trained in law before becoming a priest. His concern for people in need included the establishment of a hospital at Vicenza, while his concern for the Church led him to pursue reform through the shared life and pastoral work of priests.

In 1524 he helped found the Theatines with companions including Giovanni Pietro Carafa, the future Pope Paul IV. Their vocation combined religious discipline with active ministry. After the sack of Rome, Cajetan’s work continued in other Italian cities, including Venice and Naples. He died in Naples in 1547 and was canonized in 1671.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Cajetan

callistus-i.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
callistus-i.name: Callistus I
biography: Callistus rose from slavery to become a deacon and eventually bishop of Rome. Under Pope Zephyrinus he was entrusted with responsibilities that included the Christian cemetery now associated with his name. He became pope in 217.

Much of the surviving information about him comes from his opponent Hippolytus, so allegations about his earlier life and leadership need to be read with attention to that hostility. His papacy was marked by disputes over church discipline and the reconciliation of sinners. He is venerated as a martyr, with a commemoration on October 14.

sources.title: Vatican News: San Calisto I

camillus-de-lellis.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
camillus-de-lellis.name: Camillus de Lellis
biography: Camillus served as a soldier before turning toward religious life. A persistent leg wound prevented his attempts to remain with the Capuchins and brought him into contact with hospital care in Rome. His experience helped direct his vocation toward people who were sick.

He founded the community known as the Camillians, whose commitment included service to the sick alongside the usual religious vows. Their red cross on the habit became a sign of that dedication. Camillus emphasized personal attention, compassion, and care for spiritual as well as physical needs. He died in Rome on July 14, 1614.

sources.title: Vatican News: Saint Camille de Lellis

canute.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
canute.name: Canute IV of Denmark
biography: Canute IV, also called Cnut, became king of Denmark around 1080. His rule combined support for the Church with efforts to strengthen royal authority. Resistance to taxation and royal policy contributed to a revolt against him.

He was killed with his brother Benedict and other companions in the church of Saint Alban on Funen on July 10, 1086. The Church subsequently honored him as a martyr. January 19 is his commemoration in the older Roman calendar cited here, while July 10 is his death anniversary. He should not be confused with other Scandinavian rulers named Canute.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Canute IV

casimir.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
casimir.name: Casimir
biography: Casimir was a prince of the Polish-Lithuanian royal family. His position placed him within dynastic ambitions and plans for political marriages, but Catholic tradition remembers him particularly for his devotion and resistance to the attractions of status and luxury.

He declined an arranged marriage and did not take the Hungarian crown that had been sought for him. He died at only twenty-five, leaving a reputation for religious commitment rather than a long reign. The Church honors him as a patron of Lithuania and commemorates him on March 4.

sources.title: Vatican News: March 4 calendar

adrian.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
adrian.name: Adrian of Nicomedia
biography: Adrian, also called Hadrian, is venerated as a martyr of Nicomedia. His traditional story describes an imperial officer moved by the courage of imprisoned Christians, who declared himself a Christian and shared their fate. His wife Natalia is remembered for supporting him and the other prisoners.

The surviving martyrdom accounts contain legendary details and cannot establish every scene as historical fact. September 8 commemorates the translation of his relics in the Roman tradition; Eastern calendars also remember him on August 26. Adrian and Hadrian are alternative forms of the same name, not evidence of two separate martyrs in this account.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: Hadrian

apollonia.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
apollonia.name: Apollonia of Alexandria
biography: Apollonia was killed during anti-Christian violence in Alexandria shortly before the persecution of Decius. Unlike many early martyr stories, an account of her suffering survives through a letter by the local bishop, Dionysius, preserved in Eusebius’s Church History.

That account describes a respected Christian woman whose teeth were broken by a mob before she died in the fire prepared for her. Later devotion connected her suffering with prayers for relief from toothache. Her story belongs to the history of Alexandria’s persecuted Christian community; later versions placing her martyrdom elsewhere should not be confused with this earlier testimony.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Apollonia

apollinaris.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
apollinaris.name: Apollinaris of Ravenna
biography: Apollinaris is honored as Ravenna’s first bishop and as a martyr. Tradition connects him with Antioch and Peter’s mission, but the evidence does not securely establish those details or an exact date for his life. Proposed chronologies place him in different periods of the early Church.

His enduring significance is visible in Ravenna’s churches and its local Christian memory. The Basilica of Sant’Apollinare in Classe was consecrated in 549, centuries after the period attributed to him. Stories of his missionary journeys, suffering, and miracles express this tradition of veneration and should be distinguished from securely dated events.

sources.title: Vatican News: Sant’Apollinare

arsenius.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
arsenius.name: Arsenius the Great
biography: Arsenius is remembered among the Desert Fathers for a life devoted to silence, prayer, and repentance. His traditional biography describes a Roman who served as a tutor at the imperial court before withdrawing to the Egyptian desert.

At Scetis, he learned the ascetic life and became known for his humility and avoidance of public attention. The sayings and stories associated with him present the contrast between courtly prominence and monastic simplicity. His chronology varies between accounts, so exact dates should be treated cautiously. Western calendars commemorate him on July 19; Eastern churches also remember him on May 8.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Arsenius
Nominis: Saint Arsène

athanasius.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
athanasius.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
biography: Athanasius served as a deacon and assistant to Bishop Alexander of Alexandria and accompanied him to the Council of Nicaea in 325. He became bishop of Alexandria in 328 and defended the council’s teaching that the Son is truly divine, of the same substance as the Father.

His opposition to Arian teaching placed him at the center of prolonged theological and political conflict. His writings on the Incarnation and his Life of Anthony helped shape both Christian doctrine and the spread of monastic ideals. He is honored as a Church Father in Eastern and Western Christianity and as a Doctor of the Church in Catholic tradition.

sources.title: Benedict XVI: Saint Athanasius of Alexandria
Vatican News: May 2 calendar

barbara.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
barbara.name: Barbara
biography: Barbara has been widely venerated as a virgin and martyr since the early medieval period. Her familiar story describes a young Christian confined by her father in a tower, confessing her faith and suffering execution. However, the surviving narratives are legendary and disagree about her location and historical setting.

Her tower and its three windows became enduring symbols in Christian art. Traditions surrounding lightning in her story contributed to her association with protection from sudden danger, and to devotion among artillerymen and miners. Her established history of veneration should be distinguished from an exact biography: neither a precise birth year nor the details of her death can be securely reconstructed.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Barbara
Vatican News: December 4 calendar

barbara-the-new-martyr.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
barbara-the-new-martyr.name: Barbara the New Martyr
biography: Barbara was a religious companion of Elizabeth who died with her during the violence of the Russian Revolution. The Orthodox Church in America’s account describes their deaths in a mineshaft in 1918 and the subsequent transfer of their remains to Jerusalem.

The two were buried in the Church of Saint Mary Magdalene in 1920. Barbara is venerated as a nun-martyr in Orthodox Christianity, with a commemoration on July 18. This profile reflects that Orthodox recognition and does not assert a separate Roman Catholic canonization. The differing July dates in accounts also require attention to the Julian and Gregorian calendars.

sources.title: Orthodox Church in America: Nun-martyr Barbara

bartholomew.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bartholomew.name: Bartholomew the Apostle
biography: Bartholomew appears in the New Testament lists of the twelve apostles. Christian tradition identifies him with Nathanael, the man Philip brought to Jesus in John’s Gospel. This identification is traditional; the Gospel itself does not explicitly say that the two names refer to the same person.

The New Testament gives no detailed account of Bartholomew’s later missionary work or death. Subsequent traditions associate him with distant missions, including India, and with martyrdom. His place among the Twelve is firmer evidence than these later itineraries. The Church celebrates his feast on August 24.

sources.title: Benedict XVI: Bartholomew, October 4, 2006
Vatican News: Feast of Saint Bartholomew

basil-the-elder.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
basil-the-elder.name: Basil the Elder
biography: Basil the Elder was a Christian teacher associated with Caesarea in Cappadocia and the husband of Emmelia. Their children included Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, Peter of Sebaste, and Macrina.

He is remembered through the religious formation of this influential family. Accounts differ in assigning persecution and exile to particular generations, so detailed chronologies require caution. He is distinct from his son Basil the Great, the bishop and theologian. Basil and Emmelia are commemorated on May 30.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Basil the Great, family background

bede-the-venerable.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bede-the-venerable.name: Bede the Venerable
biography: Bede entered the care of the monastery of Wearmouth and Jarrow as a child and spent his life there in study, teaching, writing, and prayer. Ordained a priest at thirty, he drew on the monastery’s libraries to produce works of biblical interpretation, history, and the learning of his time.

His Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in 731, is an important source for early English Christianity and includes his own account of his life. His work on the calculation of Easter also influenced medieval learning. The title Venerable reflects his longstanding reputation; Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1899.

sources.title: Vatican News: Saint Bède le Vénérable

benedict.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
benedict.name: Benedict of Nursia
biography: Benedict withdrew from study in Rome to pursue religious life, first in solitude near Subiaco and later in communities of monks. He is especially associated with Monte Cassino and the Rule of Saint Benedict, which shaped monastic life across Western Europe.

The Rule joins communal prayer, reading, work, hospitality, and obedience under an abbot. Its influence is more securely documented than every episode in Benedict’s personal story, whose principal ancient narrative is Gregory the Great’s Dialogues. Benedict’s legacy includes communities that offered spiritual formation and practical care to travelers and neighbors. He is honored as a patron of Europe.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Benedict, Abbot, Patron of Europe
Franciscan Media: Saint Benedict

benedict-the-moor.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
benedict-the-moor.name: Benedict the African
biography: Benedict, traditionally also called Benedict the Moor, was a Sicilian religious of African ancestry. After living with a group of hermits, he joined the Franciscan community and became known for prayer, practical service, and the ability to guide others.

Although a religious brother rather than a priest, he served as novice master and guardian among the friars in Palermo. After holding authority, he returned to work in the kitchen. His life illustrates how leadership and ordinary service could belong to the same vocation. Canonized in 1807, he is honored particularly among African Americans. His liturgical feast is April 4.

sources.title: Franciscan Media: Saint Benedict the African

benezet.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
benezet.name: Bénézet
biography: Bénézet, a form of the name Benedict, is remembered for his part in the construction of the medieval bridge across the Rhône at Avignon. Local church tradition describes a young shepherd who gathered support for the work and linked it with care for travelers, pilgrims, and people in need.

He died before the bridge was completed and was buried in its chapel. Stories of a heavenly command and miraculous feats belong to the legend surrounding the project. The existence of the bridge and Bénézet’s historical identity are better established than every detail of those stories or the organization of the medieval bridge-building brotherhoods.

benignus.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
benignus.name: Benignus of Armagh
biography: Benignus, also known as Benén, is remembered in Irish Christian tradition as a disciple and companion of Patrick. Accounts describe his musical gifts and his contribution to worship, giving him the reputation of Patrick’s psalm-singer.

He is associated with leadership at Armagh and the transmission of the early Irish Church’s traditions. Claims that he compiled particular legal or literary works require more caution than the broad account of his devotion. The Catholic Encyclopedia also distinguishes him from another Benignus associated with Kilbannon: similar names have contributed to confusion between their stories.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Benignus

bernadette-soubirous.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bernadette-soubirous.name: Bernadette Soubirous
biography: Bernadette was born in Lourdes in 1844 and grew up amid poverty and ill health. She became known for reporting apparitions of the Virgin Mary in 1858, events that gave rise to the Lourdes pilgrimage tradition.

In 1866 she left Lourdes for the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she lived as a religious sister until her death on April 16, 1879. Her canonization in 1933 concerned the holiness of her response and life, rather than simply the fact that she reported visions. She is commemorated on April 16, with an additional February 18 celebration in the Lourdes tradition.

sources.title: Sanctuary of Lourdes: Birth and baptism of Bernadette
Sanctuary of Lourdes: Fête de Sainte Bernadette

bibiana.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
bibiana.name: Bibiana
bibiana.dates: Venerated at Rome by the fifth century
biography: Bibiana, also called Viviana, is venerated as a Roman martyr. The earliest reliable evidence for her cult is the Liber Pontificalis, which records a basilica dedicated to her under Pope Simplicius in the fifth century.

That evidence establishes an early church and veneration of her remains, but does not provide a detailed life or securely identify the circumstances of her death. Later narratives about her parents, sister, and persecution under Julian belong to a legendary account. Her December 2 commemoration preserves the memory of a martyr whose personal history remains largely unknown.

anselm-of-canterbury.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anselm-of-canterbury.name: Anselm of Canterbury
biography: Anselm entered the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy in 1060, became its prior, and succeeded Herluin as abbot in 1078. Alongside teaching and caring for his community, he wrote the Monologion and Proslogion, exploring the relationship between faith and reason.

Consecrated archbishop of Canterbury in 1093, he faced disputes with the English crown over church authority. His theological work continued amid these conflicts, including Cur Deus Homo, on the Incarnation and redemption. His surviving letters and the biography by his contemporary Eadmer provide substantial evidence for his life. The Church remembers him as a Doctor of the Church.

Vatican News: April 21 calendar

ansgar.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
ansgar.name: Ansgar
biography: Ansgar, also called Anschar or Oskar, was a Benedictine monk associated with Corbie and its foundation in Westphalia. He undertook missions to Denmark and Sweden, establishing Christian communities in places where their survival depended on changing political conditions.

He became bishop of Hamburg and continued his work after the city was destroyed in 845. His ministry subsequently connected Hamburg with Bremen. His legacy rests on sustained missionary work through setbacks, rather than on an immediate conversion of all Scandinavia. The Catholic calendar commemorates him on February 3.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Anschar
Vatican News: February 3 calendar

andrew.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
andrew.name: Andrew the Apostle
biography: Andrew was a fisherman from Bethsaida and the brother of Simon Peter. John’s Gospel presents him as a disciple of John the Baptist who followed Jesus and brought his brother to meet him. Other Gospel passages show Andrew drawing attention to the boy with loaves and fish and helping bring Greek visitors to Jesus.

The New Testament records his place among the apostles but does not narrate his death. Accounts of his later missions and martyrdom at Patras belong to subsequent Christian tradition. The familiar diagonal cross is part of that devotional history; its details should not be treated as eyewitness information from the Gospels.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Andrew, Apostle

andrew-dung-lac.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
andrew-dung-lac.name: Andrew Dũng Lạc
biography: Andrew Dũng Lạc grew up in a poor family in northern Vietnam and encountered Christianity after moving to Hanoi. A catechist provided him with housing and instruction; he received baptism and was ordained a priest in 1823.

During persecution under Emperor Minh Mạng, parishioners secured his release from an initial arrest. He changed his name and continued his ministry, but was arrested again with the priest Peter Thi. They were executed in Hanoi on December 21, 1839. Andrew belongs to the 117 Vietnamese martyrs canonized in 1988. Their shared November 24 memorial is distinct from his individual death anniversary.

sources.title: Vatican News: Andrew Dũng Lạc and companions

anne.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anne.name: Anne
anne.origin: Traditionally associated with the Holy Land
biography: Anne is the traditional name of Mary’s mother and Jesus’ grandmother. The canonical Gospels do not name Mary’s parents. The names Anne and Joachim, and stories about their longing for a child, come from early noncanonical Christian writings, especially the Protoevangelium of James.

Those writings influenced Christian devotion and art, but do not establish a documented chronology of Anne’s life. Her importance in Catholic devotion centers on Mary’s family and the transmission of faith between generations. The Church celebrates Anne and Joachim together on July 26; precise birth dates and elaborate family histories should be treated with caution.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Anne
Vatican News: Joachim and Anne

anthony-of-padua.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anthony-of-padua.name: Anthony of Padua
biography: Born Fernando in Lisbon, Anthony first joined the Augustinian Canons and studied Scripture and the Church Fathers at Coimbra. Encountering the relics of Franciscan missionaries killed in Morocco led him to join the Friars Minor in 1220. Illness interrupted his own mission to Morocco, and he subsequently reached Italy.

His learning and preaching brought him into ministry in Italy and France. With Francis of Assisi’s approval, he taught theology to the friars, connecting study with their religious life. He also served as a provincial superior before withdrawing near Padua. He died on June 13, 1231. His teaching and surviving sermons offer a fuller picture of him than miracle stories alone.

sources.title: Benedict XVI: Saint Anthony of Padua, February 10, 2010

anthony-the-great.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anthony-the-great.name: Anthony the Great
biography: Anthony became one of the most influential figures in early Egyptian monasticism. According to the Life attributed to Athanasius, hearing Jesus’ call to sell possessions and follow him prompted Anthony to distribute his inheritance and adopt a life of prayer and self-denial.

He learned from other ascetics before withdrawing farther into the desert. Disciples gathered around him and sought his guidance, even as he continued to value solitude. The dramatic accounts of his temptations belong to the spiritual narrative of his Life. Although often called the father of monasticism, he was not the first Christian ascetic, and his form of life differed from Pachomius’s organized communities.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Anthony
Vatican News: January 17 calendar

augustine-of-canterbury.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
augustine-of-canterbury.name: Augustine of Canterbury
biography: Augustine was a monk and prior of Saint Andrew’s monastery in Rome when Pope Gregory the Great chose him to lead a mission to the English. His companions entered a kingdom where Queen Bertha already practiced Christianity, and King Æthelberht permitted their work from Canterbury.

As the first archbishop of Canterbury, Augustine helped establish the structures of the English Church and remained in correspondence with Gregory. Christianity had existed in Britain before this mission, so he should not be described as bringing the faith to an entirely unchristian island. His work belongs especially to the conversion of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms. He is distinct from Augustine of Hippo.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Augustine of Canterbury
Vatican News: May 27 calendar

augustine-of-hippo.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
augustine-of-hippo.name: Augustine of Hippo
biography: Augustine studied and taught rhetoric in North Africa before pursuing his career in Rome and Milan. His search for truth included a period with the Manichaeans. In Milan, the preaching of Bishop Ambrose and Augustine’s reading of Scripture helped lead him toward baptism in 387.

After returning to North Africa, he established a religious community and was later ordained a priest at Hippo, where he eventually became bishop. His pastoral responsibilities and extensive writings brought together biblical interpretation, philosophical inquiry, and reflection on his own conversion. His Confessions remains a central witness to that spiritual journey. His life should not be confused with that of Augustine of Canterbury.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Augustine

augustine-zhao-rong.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
augustine-zhao-rong.name: Augustine Zhao Rong
biography: Augustine Zhao Rong was a Chinese soldier whose encounter with Bishop John Gabriel Taurin Dufresse helped lead him to Christianity. After baptism, he entered formation and became a diocesan priest, serving during a period of restrictions and persecution.

He was arrested, tortured, and died in 1815. Pope John Paul II canonized him with 119 other martyrs of China in 2000. The group includes Chinese laypeople and clergy as well as missionaries from abroad, killed across several centuries. Their shared memorial is July 9; it is not a claim that all 120 died on that date.

sources.title: Holy See: Augustine Zhao Rong and 119 companions
Vatican News: July 9 calendar

anuarite-nengapeta.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anuarite-nengapeta.name: Marie-Clémentine Anuarite Nengapeta
biography: Marie-Clémentine Anuarite Nengapeta was a Congolese religious sister of the Holy Family at Bafwabaka. She entered religious life despite initial obstacles and devoted herself to service within her community.

She was killed on December 1, 1964, during the violence of the Simba rebellion. The Church recognizes her death as martyrdom, and John Paul II beatified her during his 1985 visit to Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. She is identified here as Blessed Anuarite, in keeping with the cited Church sources. Accounts differ over her early chronology, so an exact birth year is not asserted.

sources.title: Vatican News: Sixty years since Anuarite’s martyrdom
John Paul II: Qui autem perseveraverit, 1985

abraham.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
abraham.name: Abraham of Kiduna
biography: Abraham of Kiduna is remembered as a priest and hermit near Edessa. According to the account preserved by Nominis, he left a prosperous family and an intended marriage for a life of prayer. After ordination, he ministered to the people of Beth-Kiduna before returning to solitude.

His tradition connects him with Ephrem the Syrian, who praised his life. This entry concerns the fourth-century hermit, not the biblical patriarch Abraham. March 16 is a local commemoration; the source does not establish the former catalog’s claims of patronage over converts and monks.

adelaide-of-italy.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
adelaide-of-italy.name: Adelaide of Italy
biography: Adelaide of Burgundy became queen of Italy through her marriage to Lothair. After his death, she resisted a marriage imposed by Berengar of Ivrea, endured imprisonment, and escaped. She subsequently married Otto I and was crowned empress with him in Rome in 962.

Her responsibilities included advising her son and governing during her grandson’s minority. Alongside this political work, she supported monasteries, the Cluniac reform, and assistance to people in need. She spent her final years at Seltz, where she died in 999. Pope Urban II canonized her in 1097; her commemoration is December 16.

sources.title: Vatican City State: Saint Adelaide, Empress

adrian-of-canterbury.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
adrian-of-canterbury.name: Adrian of Canterbury
biography: Adrian was an African-born abbot serving near Naples when Pope Vitalian considered him for Canterbury. Adrian declined the archbishopric and recommended Theodore instead. He accompanied Theodore’s mission to England, although detention in Francia delayed his arrival.

At Canterbury he became abbot of the monastery associated with Augustine and helped Theodore develop the English Church’s learning and organization. His teaching joined religious studies with wider scholarship, making Canterbury an important educational center. He died in 710 after decades in England and is commemorated on January 9.

sources.title: Catholic Encyclopedia: St. Adrian of Canterbury

afra.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
afra.name: Afra of Augsburg
afra.feast_note: August 7 in Augsburg; August 5 also appears in martyrological tradition.
biography: Afra is an early Christian martyr associated with Augsburg and the persecution of Diocletian around 304. Her grave became a place of veneration, providing evidence of an established Christian community in the Roman settlement.

Accounts of her earlier life and conversion developed over time. Both the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Diocese of Augsburg distinguish her martyrdom from later legendary embellishments; those stories should not be treated as a securely documented personal history. Augsburg commemorates her on August 7, while August 5 also occurs in martyrological tradition.

sources.title: Diocese of Augsburg: Afra

agatha.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
agatha.name: Agatha
biography: Agatha is venerated as a virgin martyr of Sicily. Her traditional account places her suffering at Catania during the persecution associated with Emperor Decius. Refusing to abandon her Christian commitment, she endured imprisonment and torture; her death is traditionally dated to February 5, 251.

The detailed dialogues, miraculous healing, and protection against Mount Etna’s lava belong to her martyrdom narrative and devotional tradition. They should be distinguished from independently documented events. Her relics and continuing veneration connect her especially with Catania, whose patron saint she is.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Agatha, Virgin and Martyr

agnes.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
agnes.name: Agnes of Rome
agnes.dates: Early Christian era; traditionally died about 304
biography: Agnes is one of Rome’s early Christian martyrs, remembered for her dedication to Christ and refusal to abandon her faith. Her surviving accounts were written after her death and differ in important details, including the period of persecution. Her traditional association with the early fourth century should not obscure that uncertainty.

Her burial place on the Via Nomentana became a center of devotion. She is frequently depicted with a lamb, and her January 21 feast is associated with the blessing of lambs whose wool is used for archbishops’ pallia. This continuing custom expresses her enduring place in Roman Christian memory.

sources.title: Vatican News: Sant’Agnese, vergine e martire

agnes-of-assisi.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
agnes-of-assisi.name: Agnes of Assisi
agnes-of-assisi.feast_note: November 19 in the Franciscan tradition; November 16 in other calendars.
biography: Agnes, born Caterina, followed her older sister Clare into religious life despite family opposition. At San Damiano she shared the Poor Ladies’ commitment to prayer and poverty. She later led the community at Monticelli near Florence and helped extend this form of life beyond Assisi.

She returned to San Damiano near the end of Clare’s life and died in November 1253. Accounts of miraculous resistance to relatives trying to remove her from the monastery belong to her devotional tradition. November 19 is her Franciscan celebration; November 16, the date of her death, appears in other calendars.

agnes-of-bohemia.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
agnes-of-bohemia.name: Agnes of Bohemia
biography: Agnes was a daughter of King Přemysl Ottokar I of Bohemia. After years of proposed dynastic marriages, she sought papal support for her decision to pursue religious life. Inspired by Clare of Assisi, she used royal resources to establish a hospital and a community of Poor Sisters in Prague.

She entered the monastery in 1234 and served as abbess, joining care for the poor with a demanding life of prayer and communal poverty. She also worked with Clare toward recognition of their form of religious life. Agnes died on March 2, 1282, and John Paul II canonized her on November 12, 1989.

alban.name: Alban
alban.feast_note: Commemorated on June 22 at St Albans Cathedral.
biography: Alban is honored as Britain’s first Christian martyr. The tradition preserved at his shrine describes him sheltering a Christian priest in Roman Verulamium, learning about the priest’s faith, and exchanging clothes with him when the authorities arrived.

Arrested in the priest’s place, Alban refused to renounce his new faith and was executed on the hillside associated with the present cathedral. His story centers on hospitality, conversion, and accepting danger to protect another person. The cathedral places the story in the early third century, but the precise chronology is not securely established.

biography: Aidan was an Irish monk associated with Iona who became a missionary bishop in Northumbria. Supported by King Oswald, he established his center at Lindisfarne and taught Christianity through patient instruction and a deliberately simple way of life.

The tradition recorded by Bede emphasizes his generosity, concern for the poor, and willingness to travel among the people he served. He died near Bamburgh on August 31, 651. The catalog’s entries “Aidan” and “Aidan of Lindisfarne” describe the same person; May 6 is not supported as his feast by the cited sources.

biography: Albert the Great, also called Albertus Magnus, was a Dominican scholar whose work ranged from theology and philosophy to the natural world. He taught Thomas Aquinas and helped bring Aristotle’s writings into the intellectual life of medieval Latin Christianity.

He served as a Dominican provincial and briefly as bishop of Regensburg, while continuing his teaching and study. Albert died in Cologne on November 15, 1280. albert-chmielowski.name: Albert Chmielowski
biography: Born Adam Chmielowski, Albert was a Polish artist who lost a leg after being wounded in the uprising of 1863. He pursued painting, explored a Jesuit vocation, and eventually embraced Franciscan spirituality. His encounter with the conditions of homeless people in Kraków changed the direction of his life.

Taking the name Brother Albert, he chose to live among the people he served. He founded communities of brothers and sisters devoted to shelter and care for those in need, extending this work despite his disability. He died in a Kraków shelter on Christmas Day 1916. John Paul II canonized him on November 12, 1989.

biography: Albert came from a Norman family and was brought to Montecorvino as a child. He became the community’s bishop and was remembered for holiness, pastoral service, and traditions of visions and miracles.

The available short accounts disagree about when he lost his sight, so a precise chronology of his blindness is not established here. His death is recorded in 1127 and his feast on April 5. The former April 19 date is not supported by the references consulted.

biography: Alberto Hurtado experienced poverty after his father’s death. He supported his family while studying law before entering the Jesuits in 1923. Ordained in 1933, he returned to Chile as a teacher, spiritual director, and advocate for a faith expressed in social responsibility.

In 1944 his appeal on behalf of homeless people helped launch Hogar de Cristo, which developed homes, educational initiatives, and care for people in need. He also promoted workers’ organization informed by Catholic social teaching and founded the journal Mensaje. He died on August 18, 1952. His work joined formation of laypeople with practical service to those excluded from secure housing and opportunity.

biography: Alexander Nevsky was a medieval prince associated with Novgorod and the defense of the Russian lands. His life combined military leadership, dynastic responsibilities, and political relations with surrounding powers. The Orthodox Church in America preserves an extensive devotional account of his life.

He died in 1263 and is commemorated in the Eastern Orthodox tradition on November 23, with a separate August 30 observance associated with the translation of his relics. alexander-of-jerusalem.name: Alexander of Jerusalem
biography: Alexander became bishop of Jerusalem after serving as a coadjutor there. Educated in the Christian intellectual world associated with Alexandria, he supported theological learning and established a library in Jerusalem.

He defended and supported Origen’s teaching, participating in the controversies surrounding that influential theologian. Alexander also endured imprisonment during persecution. He died in captivity at Caesarea around 250 and is venerated as a martyr. Vatican News commemorates him on May 16; the previous catalog’s February 26 date was not confirmed by that source.

biography: Alexius, also spelled Alexis, is associated with the story of the Man of God of Edessa. The Catholic Encyclopedia traces his Western devotion to an earlier Eastern tradition, rather than treating every detail of the later Roman narrative as contemporary biography.

The developed legend describes a wealthy Roman who left marriage and status for poverty, eventually returning unrecognized to his family’s household. His story became influential as an image of humility and renunciation. Its literary development matters: the precise dates and dramatic household episodes should be presented as tradition, not established personal records.

all-saints.name: All Saints
biography: All Saints is the Catholic solemnity honoring the saints together. It celebrates the holiness of those who share life with God and invites the faithful to seek their intercession. It is a liturgical observance, not the biography of a person named “All Saints.”

The celebration falls on November 1. In the Latin Rite dioceses of the United States it is generally a holy day of obligation, with the exceptions specified by the bishops’ conference when it falls on Saturday or Monday. It should be distinguished from All Souls’ Day, the following day’s commemoration of the faithful departed.

all-souls.name: All Souls
biography: All Souls’ Day is the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed, observed on November 2. Catholics pray for those who have died, expressing hope in Christ’s resurrection and commending the departed to God’s mercy.

This is a collective liturgical commemoration, not an individual saint. It follows All Saints’ Day but has a distinct focus: prayer for the deceased rather than a celebration of the saints already honored in heaven. A directory entry should explain that distinction instead of assigning a personal life story or invented quotations to “All Souls.”

alphonsa-of-the-immaculate-conception.name: Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception
biography: Alphonsa was born Annakutty Muttathupadathu in Kerala and raised in the Syro-Malabar Catholic tradition. After losing her mother in infancy, she was cared for by relatives. She pursued religious life and became a Franciscan Clarist sister at Bharananganam.

Her adult life was marked by repeated illness. Her canonization biography presents her prayer, charity, and perseverance through suffering as central to her witness. She died on July 28, 1946, was beatified in 1986, and was canonized in 2008. Her life belongs to the long Christian history of India and especially to its Eastern Catholic heritage.

alphonsus-liguori.name: Alphonsus Liguori
biography: Alphonsus Liguori trained as a lawyer before becoming a priest in 1726. His ministry focused on people with limited access to religious formation, especially the poor and rural communities. He founded the congregation now known as the Redemptorists to support that mission.

As a preacher, confessor, composer, and writer on moral theology, he sought to make Christian teaching accessible. He also served as bishop of Sant’Agata dei Goti. Canonized in 1839 and named a Doctor of the Church in 1871, he is commemorated on August 1. “Alphonsus Maria de Liguori” is another form of his name, not a separate saint.

aloysius-gonzaga.name: Aloysius Gonzaga
biography: Aloysius, also known as Luigi Gonzaga, was born into a ruling Italian family and prepared for a privileged public life. His growing commitment to prayer brought him into conflict with those expectations. He eventually renounced his inheritance to enter the Society of Jesus.

During an epidemic he cared for sick people and contracted the illness himself. He died on June 21, 1591, while still a young Jesuit. His story is remembered for the practical consequences of his vocation: relinquishing status and accepting personal risk in service to people whose needs could easily have been ignored.

ambrose.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
ambrose.name: Ambrose of Milan
biography: Ambrose was a Roman governor when a disputed episcopal election in Milan unexpectedly brought him forward as the people’s choice. Still a catechumen, he had to receive baptism before becoming bishop in 374. His administrative experience became part of a demanding pastoral vocation.

As bishop he defended the Church’s teaching about Christ, cared for people in need, and contributed to theology and liturgical hymnody. His importance extends beyond the circumstances of his election: he is honored as a Doctor of the Church. His December 7 commemoration is associated with his becoming bishop, rather than an assumed date of death.

sources.title: Vatican News: St. Ambrose, Bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church

anastasia.name: Anastasia of Sirmium
biography: Anastasia is venerated as a martyr associated with Sirmium during the persecution of Diocletian. Vatican News recounts her assistance to persecuted Christians and her refusal to abandon her faith when arrested.

Her devotional narrative includes escape from a damaged ship, recapture, and death by burning. These episodes are presented as the tradition of her martyrdom rather than a fully documented modern biography. The Catholic commemoration cited here is December 25.

andr-bessette.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
andr-bessette.name: André Bessette
andr-bessette.feast_note: January 7 at Saint Joseph’s Oratory in Canada; local calendars may differ.
biography: Born Alfred Bessette, Brother André served as porter at Collège Notre-Dame in Montreal. His work put him in contact with people seeking help, comfort, and prayer. He encouraged devotion to Saint Joseph and became closely associated with the place of pilgrimage that developed on Mount Royal.

The oratory preserves accounts of healings attributed to intercession and the history of his cause. Benedict XVI canonized him on October 17, 2010. He died on January 6, 1937, but the oratory identifies January 7 as his liturgical feast; the anniversary of a saint’s death and a local celebration need not be identical.

andrew-kim-taegon.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
andrew-kim-taegon.name: Andrew Kim Taegon
biography: Andrew Kim Taegon became the first native-born Korean Catholic priest. Baptized as a teenager, he traveled to Macau for formation and was ordained in Shanghai. He returned to minister to a Korean community that had grown through the initiative of lay believers despite persecution.

His ministry in Korea was brief: he was arrested and killed on September 16, 1846. His witness is commemorated with Paul Chong Hasang and their companions on September 20. The distinction between his death date and the group memorial explains why both September dates appear in accounts of his life.

angela-merici.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
angela-merici.name: Angela Merici
biography: Angela Merici grew up near Lake Garda and developed a strong religious life from childhood. After family bereavements, she became a Franciscan tertiary and joined prayer with practical works of mercy. Her ministry later brought her to Brescia.

She founded the Company of Saint Ursula, opening a distinctive path for women to dedicate their lives to God while remaining active in the world. Her legacy developed through the Ursuline tradition and its service to women and girls. The Church commemorates her on January 27; she was canonized in 1807.

anicetus.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anicetus.name: Anicetus
anicetus.feast_note: April 20 in Vatican News; April 17 occurs in older references.
biography: Anicetus was a second-century bishop of Rome, originally from Syria. Exact dates for his pontificate differ in early chronologies, so a narrowly specified sequence of years can imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

He is especially remembered for discussing the date of Easter with Polycarp of Smyrna. Their communities followed different practices, but they maintained fellowship without resolving the disagreement. Vatican News commemorates him on April 20. Older references also record April 17 and other dates; those differences should be identified rather than silently conflated.

anna-wang.name: Anna Wang
anna-wang.feast_note: Group memorial and individual death date require separate calendar documentation.
anna-wang.dates: Died at about fourteen years of age
biography: Anna Wang was a young Chinese Christian remembered among the martyrs canonized by John Paul II on October 1, 2000. In the canonization homily, the pope recalled her refusal to renounce her faith despite threats of execution.

Her witness belongs to the wider history of the 120 martyrs of China, which includes laypeople as well as clergy and religious. The cited homily establishes her recognition and the central account of her martyrdom; it does not substantiate every biographical detail or patronage previously assigned to her in the catalog.

anne-catherine-emmerich.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
anne-catherine-emmerich.name: Anne Catherine Emmerich
anne-catherine-emmerich.feast_note: Liturgical memorial listed by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints.
biography: Anne Catherine Emmerich, also spelled Emmerick, came from a poor farming family and became known for a deeply contemplative religious life. Her devotion centered especially on the Passion of Christ and on prayer amid suffering.

John Paul II beatified her on October 3, 2004, praising her charity and interior life. The appropriate title supported by that act is Blessed. Accounts of mystical experiences should be distinguished from publicly verifiable historical events; beatification should not be presented as a blanket verification of every narrative later associated with her.

ansbert.review_method: AI-assisted comparison with the cited external sources; not ecclesiastical approval
ansbert.name: Ansbert of Rouen
biography: Ansbert served as abbot of Fontenelle before becoming bishop of Rouen. His career belongs to the Church of the early medieval Frankish kingdoms, where monastic leadership and episcopal service were closely connected.

According to Nominis, he was exiled by Pepin of Herstal and died at Hautmont on the Sambre around 695. The source records a local feast on February 9. The catalog’s earlier April 21 date and unsourced personal sayings are not established by this account.
